If she does not call, this lead does not exist.
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The call went straight from 'How can I help you?' into calendar-checking.

Floors and stairs never asked — on a move between two apartment complexes. Not the floor at 1615 Royal Crest, not the floor at 14501 East Riverside, not whether either building has an elevator. On an apartment-to-apartment move this is the largest single time variable and it was never touched.

Packing needs never asked. He inferred it instead: 'like there won't be any boxes or anything like that either you, that'll, you'll move that on your own' — which is a guess the customer never actually confirmed, folded into the sentence where he endorsed the 2.5 hour minimum.
Box count never asked.

Access concerns never asked. No elevator, no parking, no gate code, no loading-zone question, on a move between two Austin apartment complexes where both ends are almost certainly constrained.

Moving stressors never asked. The customer opened with 'I wanna move tomorrow. Do you think it's possible if I book it right now?' — a same-day urgency signal that was answered operationally (no availability) and never explored.

Hourly rate given as a team rate, not per mover per hour. No sense-check anywhere. Three repetitions of the same question is the clearest possible signal that the explanation had not landed, and it never triggered a 'let me lay this out a different way' or a 'does that make sense?'
Drive time never mentioned. 1615 Royal Crest to 14501 East Riverside is a real cross-town Austin haul and it is billable time, on a job being sized at the 2.5 hour minimum.
Walk distance never asked at either end, and no equivalents used.

Assembly and disassembly never raised — on a move with three beds. Three teardowns and three rebuilds is a substantial share of a 2.5 hour minimum and nobody established whether the beds even come apart.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. She told him 'we have a lot of people here and the thing is, we actually only need the truck and the driver' — a customer who is already planning to do most of the labor herself. The prep and consolidation speech is the single most useful thing anyone could have said to her, and it would have made the 2.5 hour minimum genuinely achievable instead of merely agreed to.

Zero booking attempt — 0/11 on the whole section. She had accepted the Saturday slot out loud ('Yeah, I think we can for Saturday morning') and confirmed the arrival window, and the call still ended with 'Yeah, we'll be here if you need us.' No offer to hold the slot, no 'want me to pencil that in?', no specific follow-up time.
No deposit required never mentioned — the exact answer to 'I'll call you back after I call my friend.' Locking a Saturday morning slot costs her nothing and she never learned that.
No email handoff at all — no confirmation offered, no email address collected, no bolded details, no correction ask.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or callback number. 'We'll be here' is not hours and not a number.
top_strength: Jespah's best instinct on this call was to widen the search before he delivered bad news. Asked for a next-day move, he did not check one calendar — 'I'm looking at both of our Austin branches to kinda cast a wide net for you' — and then delivered the miss with an alternative and a question attached rather than a flat no: 'unfortunately tomorrow, both north and south Austin offices are booked out. We have our earliest availability is Saturday morning. Is that helpful to us? Is that too late for you?' That last question is the right one, and it worked: the customer went from wanting tomorrow to 'Yeah, I think we can for Saturday morning' inside a minute. His inclusions list is also unusually complete and specific for a rate-shopper call — asked whether $222 covers the driver, he gave her the whole picture in one pass: 'that includes everything. So it includes the crew, the truck taxes, liability coverage all of the materials we use to move and protect everything like, you know, blankets and shrink wrap dollies and hand trucks, stair and floor protection. Even any tools we may need for disassemble or reassembly. So it includes everything that we'll need.' He paired it with a clean fee denial — 'there are zero additional fees on top of that' — which is the differentiator a price-shopper actually needs. The strongest single moment is the budget accommodation. Faced with a customer trying to buy one hour against a 2.5 hour minimum, he did not just repeat the rule; he found her a way to spend less: 'if you want we can just set you up with only that amount of time move, you know, the biggest heaviest items first move what we can within that time and anything that's left behind you can move on your own.' That is real problem-solving for a price-sensitive caller, and it is the moment she stopped negotiating and started planning. He also stayed patient and non-defensive across three repetitions of the same question from a customer working through a language barrier, and never once made her feel like she was being difficult.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is not a subtle one: this call has no lead record. Seven minutes, a customer who accepted a Saturday slot out loud, and Jespah has no name, no email, no phone, no address beyond two partial street lines. The whole call is stored in her memory. Get the name in the first thirty seconds — 'Happy to check Saturday for you, who am I speaking with?' — and the email before any number leaves his mouth. Second priority, and worth the sale: she accepted Saturday and he let her hang up. 'I'll call you back after I call my friend' is a commitment-risk objection, and the answer is sitting unused in the Einstein script: 'Absolutely, check with them. One thing that helps — there's no deposit and no card on file to book, so I can hold Saturday morning for you right now at no cost, and if the plan changes you just call and I'll release it. What's the best email for you? I'll send the details over so you both can look at the same thing.' That is the booking attempt, the no-deposit differentiator, and the email capture in three sentences, and this call scored 0/11 without them. Third: probe. Section 2 scored 1/9, the lowest in the week's sample. He learned the residence type and the bedroom counts and nothing else — no floors, no elevator, no parking, no boxes, no packing, no walk, no stops, no special items, on a move between two Austin apartment complexes. That is not a shortage of time; the call had room. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review, and this one runs the opposite direction from the usual pattern: this is an underestimate on an apartment, which is the second half of the failure mode Cameron and Amanda identified. The customer proposed the job could be done in about an hour, and Jespah agreed it fits the minimum — 'if you're moving just three beds and two sofas. I agree. I think that can all be done within the two and a half hour minimum' — without knowing what floor either apartment is on, whether either has an elevator, how far the walk is, whether the beds disassemble, how long the cross-town drive from Royal Crest to East Riverside takes, or whether her helpers will actually be there. Three bed teardowns plus three rebuilds plus a cross-town drive plus two unknown apartment walks is very plausibly over 2.5 hours on its own. Agreeing with a customer's optimistic number is as much an accuracy failure as padding against it, and it is worse commercially, because the overage lands as a surprise on move day. The fix is the same in both directions: build the number from inputs, out loud, and only then say whether it fits. Fourth, the proration explanation. She asked the same question three times and never got the piece she was missing, which is that after the 2.5 hour minimum the clock bills in fifteen-minute increments. The answer she needed was one sentence: 'The smallest we can book is two and a half hours, $555. After that we bill in fifteen-minute pieces, so if you go to two hours forty-five you pay for two forty-five, not three.' Repeating the minimum a third time was not going to get there.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely patient and never condescending with a customer working through a language barrier and asking the same question three times — 'Sure.', 'Yeah, yeah, absolutely. If you need we'll be here', 'Of course. Take care' — but the warmth stays minimal and reactive: no name ever asked or used, no empathy marker when she revealed she needed to move tomorrow, no acknowledgment of the repeated confusion, and no rapport moment anywhere in seven minutes.
audio_review_reason: Two things this transcript cannot settle. First, the customer's speech is heavily garbled throughout ('that's the acu, actually', 'that's only like a three wasn't in three bed and two. So far the small sofa deli'), so it is impossible to tell from text whether her three repeated questions came from an explanation that was genuinely unclear or from a phone-line and language barrier the rep handled well. Second, the score sits on the 3/4 boundary — his word choices read patient, but whether that patience came through in delivery or as flat, rote repetition is exactly what audio would resolve, and it changes whether this is coached as a warmth issue or a structure issue.
